# Golang Utilities

> Published task guides for Golang Utilities.


## Golang utilities guides

<!--
Copyright (C) 2020-2026 Arm Limited or its affiliates and Contributors. All rights reserved.
SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
-->

Use these task guides alongside the generated Go API reference.

- [Go modules](https://arm-software.github.io/golang-utils/guides/go-modules.html): consuming individual modules, developing with
  the repository workspace, running checks, and preparing [CDS](https://github.com/ARMmbed/continuous-delivery-scripts) releases.
- [Reusable Go multimodules actions](https://arm-software.github.io/golang-utils/guides/action-go-multimodules.html): choose the
  orchestrator or individual discovery, tool setup, command, and test/coverage actions for
  this repository or another Go project.
- [Migration guides](https://arm-software.github.io/golang-utils/guides/migrations/index.html): backward-compatible module
  refactoring and supported import-path transitions.


## Use the Go multimodules action

<!--
Copyright (C) 2020-2026 Arm Limited or its affiliates and Contributors. All rights reserved.
SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
-->

The [`go-multimodules` composite action](https://github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/tree/master/actions/go-multimodules)
orchestrates independently reusable actions for discovery, per-module commands,
and tests/coverage. They read `go.work` when present; otherwise they find
`go.mod` files directly. If a workspace omits a module, discovery fails rather
than silently skipping it. All actions use Bash and standard Go tooling. Some specific actions may rely on additional tools and dependencies though.

### Call it from this repository

This repository's workflows use:

```yaml
- uses: $/actions/go-multimodules
  with:
    task: build
```

`$/actions/...` resolves an action from the
**repository containing the workflow**, at the **same revision** as that
workflow. This keeps the workflow and action together when a reusable workflow
is called by another repository. It also lets a pull request exercise its own
changes to the action. The action lives at `actions/go-multimodules/action.yml`.

The top-level action composes `detect-go-modules`, `run-go-modules` (for
generation and lint), and `test-go-modules` (for JUnit and merged coverage).
Use it for the complete pipeline, or call any of its components on their own.

### Call it from another repository

Use a repository-qualified reference in the other repository's workflow. Pin
it to a full commit SHA or a version number available in `ARM-software/golang-utils`:

```yaml
name: Go modules
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      checks: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v7
        with:
          go-version: '1.26.1' # Choose the version required by your modules.
          cache-dependency-path: '**/go.sum'
      - uses: ARM-software/golang-utils/actions/sync-go-workspace@<full-commit-sha>
        if: ${{ hashFiles('go.work') != '' }}
      - uses: golangci/golangci-lint-action@v9
        with:
          version: latest
          install-only: true
      - uses: ARM-software/golang-utils/actions/setup-gotestsum@<full-commit-sha>
        with:
          version: v1.13.0
      - uses: ARM-software/golang-utils/actions/go-multimodules@<full-commit-sha>
        with:
          task: verify
          build-tags: integration
          artifact-prefix: '${{ github.job }}-'
```

Replace `<full-commit-sha>` with a real commit SHA or a version number from this repository. The
`$/actions/...` reference is for actions **in the workflow's repository**; in
the example above it would point at the calling repository, so the
repository-qualified reference is required instead. `artifact-prefix` is
optional; it helps prevent name collisions if several action invocations
upload reports in the same run.

### Choose an individual action

| Action | Standalone purpose | Useful inputs and outputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`detect-go-modules`](https://github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/tree/master/actions/detect-go-modules) | Verify that no module is omitted. | Outputs `modules` (newline-delimited) and `modules-json` for a matrix. |
| [`sync-go-workspace`](https://github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/tree/master/actions/sync-go-workspace) | Run `go work sync` at the checked-out repository root. | No inputs; requires Go and `go.work`. |
| [`setup-gotestsum`](https://github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/tree/master/actions/setup-gotestsum) | Install the `gotestsum` test runner and put it on `PATH`. | `version` defaults to `v1.13.0`. |
| [`run-go-modules`](https://github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/tree/master/actions/run-go-modules) | Run one task across all modules. | Set `task` to `generate`, `lint`, `build`, `download`, or `analyze`; optionally supply `modules`, `results-file`, `skip-results-file`, and `build-tags`. |
| [`test-go-modules`](https://github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/tree/master/actions/test-go-modules) | Test modules with `gotestsum`, merge coverage and publish reports. | Optionally supply `modules`, `generation-results`, `lint-results`, `artifact-prefix`, and `build-tags`; outputs `combined-coverage`. |
| [`go-multimodules`](https://github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/tree/master/actions/go-multimodules) | Compose discovery, generation, lint and testing in one call. | Set `task` (default `verify`) and optionally `build-tags`; outputs `modules-json`. |

The individual actions can be used independently. If `modules` is omitted,
`run-go-modules` and `test-go-modules` call the discovery action themselves.
In this repository use `$/actions/<name>` to call each action; from another
repository use `ARM-software/golang-utils/actions/<name>@<full-commit-sha>`.

For example, to choose the stages separately in another repository, add the
following steps after checkout, Go setup, optional workspace sync, and the
`setup-gotestsum` and `golangci-lint-action` installation steps (as in the
complete example above):

```yaml
- id: modules
  uses: ARM-software/golang-utils/actions/detect-go-modules@<full-commit-sha>
- id: generate
  continue-on-error: true
  uses: ARM-software/golang-utils/actions/run-go-modules@<full-commit-sha>
  with:
    task: generate
    build-tags: integration
    modules: ${{ steps.modules.outputs.modules }}
    results-file: artifacts/generate.tsv
- id: lint
  if: ${{ always() }}
  continue-on-error: true
  uses: ARM-software/golang-utils/actions/run-go-modules@<full-commit-sha>
  with:
    task: lint
    build-tags: integration
    modules: ${{ steps.modules.outputs.modules }}
    results-file: artifacts/lint.tsv
    skip-results-file: artifacts/generate.tsv
- id: test
  if: ${{ always() }}
  uses: ARM-software/golang-utils/actions/test-go-modules@<full-commit-sha>
  with:
    build-tags: integration
    modules: ${{ steps.modules.outputs.modules }}
    generation-results: artifacts/generate.tsv
    lint-results: artifacts/lint.tsv
    artifact-prefix: '${{ github.job }}-'
```

The TSV results allow later stages to report generation and lint failures
without concealing test results. Use the same pinned SHA/version for every component
so their interfaces stay in sync. Build, analysis, generation, lint, and tests
include the `integration` build tag by default; `download` and discovery do not
compile tagged packages. Override `build-tags` if the calling project needs
additional tags.

### Tasks and reports

| Top-level `task` | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `list` | List the modules selected from `go.work` or `go.mod` files. |
| `download` | Run `go mod download` for each module with `GOWORK=off`. |
| `build` | Build every module. |
| `analyze` | Compile tests in every module without running test cases (for CodeQL). |
| `generate` | Run `go generate` in every module. |
| `lint` | Run `golangci-lint` in every module. |
| `verify` (default) | Generate, lint and test each module with `gotestsum`; collect coverage and reports. |

`verify` calls the granular generation, lint and test actions in order. The
test action uploads one JUnit XML file and one coverage profile per module,
plus a project-wide `combined.out` coverage profile. Test results are rendered
in the workflow summary and, for same-repository pull requests, PR comments via
`EnricoMi/publish-unit-test-result-action`. The JUnit artifact keeps the raw
per-module XML plus EnricoMi's combined JSON report, while the local summary
keeps every module's generate, lint and test status, per-module coverage, and
links to the uploaded reports. Artifact uploads and summaries also run when
verification fails, so available failure reports remain accessible.

Set up Go before using any task. For `verify` or `lint`, install
`golangci-lint`; for `verify`, also install `gotestsum`. GitHub-hosted runners
provide the Bash and standard Unix tools used by the action.


## Go modules

<!--
Copyright (C) 2020-2026 Arm Limited or its affiliates and Contributors. All rights reserved.
SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
-->

This repository uses a single repository-wide `go.work` file at the repository root and a set of Go modules under `utils/`.

### Consumer usage

Depend on the specific submodule that provides the package you import.

Examples:

```bash
go get github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/http@latest
go get github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/filesystem@latest
go get github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/validation@latest
```

> **Compatibility note:** The `github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils`
> module remains a lightweight umbrella for compatibility and tooling. New
> consumers should depend on the narrower submodule they actually import.
> Submodule tags start with the next [CDS] project release; `v1.170.7` and
> earlier published only the original umbrella module.
> If using dependabot, the upgrade and change should be transparent.
>
> If your `go.mod` still requires a pre-split umbrella version such as
> `github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils v1.170.7`, first upgrade that
> requirement to the first split-aware umbrella release, then add the narrower
> module you actually import, for example
> `github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/collection`. In a local test,
> mixing `v1.170.7` with the split `collection` module caused Go to fail with:
> `ambiguous import: found package github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/collection in multiple modules`.
> Remove the umbrella requirement entirely if you no longer import packages from
> it. See [Ambiguous Imports](#ambiguous-imports) below for the generic cause
> and fix pattern.

### Ambiguous imports

Go reports an `ambiguous import` error when the build list contains two modules
that both appear to provide the same package import path.

In this repository, the most likely cause is a mixed pre-split and post-split
dependency set, for example:

- the umbrella module at a pre-split version such as
  `github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils v1.170.7`
- a newer split module such as
  `github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/collection`

In that situation, Go sees `github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/collection`
inside both modules and fails instead of guessing which one you meant.

Example error:

```text
go: example.com/my-project imports
	github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/collection: ambiguous import: found package github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/collection in multiple modules:
	github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils v1.170.7
	github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/collection v1.171.0
```

To fix it:

1. Upgrade `github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils` to the first
   split-aware umbrella release, or remove it entirely if you no longer import
   packages from that umbrella module.
2. Add or keep only the narrower modules that match the packages you actually
   import, such as `github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/collection`.
3. Run `go mod tidy` and confirm the older umbrella version no longer pulls the
   same package path into the build list.

If you still see the error, inspect `go mod graph` or `go list -m all` to find
which dependency is still selecting the older umbrella module.

### Workspace structure

- `go.work` lives at the repository root.
- `utils/` is the umbrella module.
- Each top-level consumable package under `utils/` has its own `go.mod`.
- Shared helper packages that are reused across module boundaries also have their own `go.mod` when keeping them separate prevents test-only dependencies from leaking into production modules.

CI uses the reusable `sync-go-workspace` action to run `go work sync`, then the
Go multimodules action to discover modules from `go.work`. It checks that every
`go.mod` is listed.

### Internal dependencies

Internal module dependencies must follow this pattern:

1. Add a normal `require` on the repository release version, for example `github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/commonerrors v1.170.7` while preparing the first multi-module release.
2. Add a local `replace` pointing at the sibling checkout path, for example `replace github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/commonerrors => ../commonerrors`.
3. Keep `replace` directives suitable for local development with `GOWORK=off`.

This keeps local development working before publication. [CDS] 4.8.0+ is responsible
for preparing the versioned internal requirements and tagging all workspace
modules as part of the single project release. Go consumers ignore dependency
modules' local `replace` directives and resolve versioned requirements from
published [CDS] tags.

### Adding a new module

1. Create the package directory under `utils/`.
2. Add a `go.mod` whose module path matches the import path.
3. Add the module path to the repository `go.work`.
4. Add versioned `require` plus local `replace` directives for internal dependencies.
5. If the module contains `go:generate` directives, use `go tool` and declare
   only the needed tools in that module's `tool` block.
6. Update `.github/dependabot.yml` so the new `go.mod` directory is covered.
7. Ensure CI still discovers the module from `go.work`.

If the module root would otherwise contain no Go source file, add a small `doc.go` so Go tooling can still address the module cleanly.

When splitting an existing package into a module, follow the
[backward-compatible module refactoring guide](https://arm-software.github.io/golang-utils/guides/migrations/refactoring-go-modules.html)
to preserve consumer imports and dependencies.

### Running checks across all modules

From the repository root:

```bash
go work sync
go work edit -json |
  sed -n 's/^[[:space:]]*"DiskPath": "\([^"]*\)".*$/\1/p' |
  while IFS= read -r module; do
    (cd "$module" && go generate -tags integration ./... && golangci-lint run --build-tags integration ./... && go test -tags integration ./...)
  done
```

The composite action's `verify` task runs those checks with `gotestsum`, then
produces per-module JUnit XML and coverage profiles, plus combined reports,
under `artifacts/`. Local commands use Bash on Linux and macOS; on Windows, use
WSL with Go and `golangci-lint` installed.
To confirm that one module builds without workspace resolution, run
`GOWORK=off go test ./...` from its directory.

### CI behaviour

The CI workflows call the local [Go multimodules composite action](https://arm-software.github.io/golang-utils/guides/action-go-multimodules.html)
with `uses: $/actions/go-multimodules`. It:

1. Reads the module list from the repository `go.work`.
2. Runs `go generate` per module.
3. Runs `golangci-lint` per module.
4. Runs tests per module with `gotestsum` and writes per-module and combined JUnit XML reports.
5. Writes one coverage profile per module and merges them into a combined profile.
6. Uploads JUnit and coverage artifacts.
7. Publishes a GitHub Actions summary listing each module's coverage, failed
   test cases, and links to the JUnit and coverage artifacts.

See the [Go multimodules action guide](https://arm-software.github.io/golang-utils/guides/action-go-multimodules.html) for a full
example using the action from another repository, including the difference
between `$` and a repository-qualified `uses:` reference.

### [CDS] releases

[CDS] remains the only project release mechanism.

- All modules share the same repository release version.
- Submodules are not versioned or released independently.
- `cd-tag-and-release` remains the release entry point.
- In [CDS] 4.8.0+, `cd-tag-and-release` updates versioned internal `require`
  directives and includes them in the shared release commit before tagging
  and publication. The repository's `release.yml` requires this version.

[CDS]: https://github.com/ARMmbed/continuous-delivery-scripts


## Migration guides

<!--
Copyright (C) 2020-2026 Arm Limited or its affiliates and Contributors. All rights reserved.
SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
-->

These guides describe transitions between supported APIs and import paths:

- [Replacing ozzo `validation.Required`](https://arm-software.github.io/golang-utils/guides/migrations/ozzo-required.html): preserve pre-v4.4
  zero-valued struct semantics with `utils/validation.IsRequired`.
- [Refactoring Go modules without breaking imports](https://arm-software.github.io/golang-utils/guides/migrations/refactoring-go-modules.html):
  split modules, preserve old paths, and verify compatibility.
- [Serialisation packages](https://arm-software.github.io/golang-utils/guides/migrations/serialisation.html): new import paths and existing
  compatible imports.


## Replacing ozzo `validation.Required`

<!--
Copyright (C) 2020-2026 Arm Limited or its affiliates and Contributors. All rights reserved.
SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
-->

`github.com/go-ozzo/ozzo-validation/v4` changed `Required` semantics in v4.4.0.
Zero-valued structs now count as empty, which means code that previously treated
decoded struct values as present can start failing after the upgrade.

Upstream references:

- ozzo-validation v4.4.0 release notes:
  <https://github.com/go-ozzo/ozzo-validation/releases/tag/v4.4.0>
- ozzo-validation README, "Empty Values":
  <https://github.com/go-ozzo/ozzo-validation#empty-values>

### What changed

Before ozzo v4.4.0, `validation.Required` treated most zero-valued structs as
present. After v4.4.0, zero-valued structs are considered empty.

This affects patterns like:

```go
type Flags struct {
	Enabled bool
}

type Config struct {
	Flags Flags
}

func (c Config) Validate() error {
	return validation.ValidateStruct(&c,
		validation.Field(&c.Flags, validation.Required),
	)
}
```

With newer ozzo versions, `Config{Flags: Flags{}}` now fails `validation.Required`.

### Replacement in golang-utils

Use `github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/validation.IsRequired` instead.

`IsRequired` is an alias of `IsRequiredLegacy` and preserves the older ozzo
behavior that many configuration-style validations relied on:

- nil values are rejected
- empty strings are rejected
- `time.Time{}` is rejected
- zero-valued non-time structs are still treated as present

### Migration

Replace this:

```go
import validation "github.com/go-ozzo/ozzo-validation/v4"

func (c Config) Validate() error {
	return validation.ValidateStruct(&c,
		validation.Field(&c.Flags, validation.Required),
	)
}
```

With this:

```go
import (
	ozzovalidation "github.com/go-ozzo/ozzo-validation/v4"
	utilsvalidation "github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/validation"
)

func (c Config) Validate() error {
	return ozzovalidation.ValidateStruct(&c,
		ozzovalidation.Field(&c.Flags, utilsvalidation.IsRequired),
	)
}
```

If your file already imports golang-utils validation helpers, the change is often
just:

```go
validation.Field(&cfg.Flags, validationutils.IsRequired)
```

instead of:

```go
validation.Field(&cfg.Flags, validation.Required)
```

### When to keep ozzo `validation.Required`

Keep ozzo's built-in `validation.Required` when you explicitly want zero values
to be rejected, such as:

- `false` must be rejected
- `0` must be rejected
- zero-valued structs should be treated as missing

### Rule choice summary

- Use ozzo `validation.Required` for strict non-empty semantics.
- Use `utils/validation.Required` for state-style presence semantics where `0`
  and `false` should still count as present.
- Use `utils/validation.IsRequired` to preserve pre-v4.4 ozzo behavior for
  zero-valued structs.


## Refactor Go modules without breaking imports

<!--
Copyright (C) 2020-2026 Arm Limited or its affiliates and Contributors. All rights reserved.
SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
-->

Use this guide when moving a package into its own module or replacing an old
import path with a preferred one. The goal is to keep existing consumers
working while allowing new code to depend on smaller modules and a single
implementation.

### Keep an import path when splitting a module

Adding `go.mod` inside a package directory changes which module provides that
package, even when its import path stays the same. For example, a new module at
`utils/codec/json` can retain the import path
`example.com/project/utils/codec/json`. The parent module no longer contains
that subtree at the new revision.

1. Declare the existing package import path in the new `go.mod`. Add the module
   to the repository's root `go.work` and ensure module discovery includes it.
2. Give each internal dependency a versioned `require` and a relative local
   `replace`, including dependencies between newly split modules. Test from
   each module with `GOWORK=off`: workspace resolution alone can hide a missing
   requirement or replacement. Go consumers ignore replacements in dependency
   modules, so the required versions must be published together.
3. Account for consumers that previously required only the parent module.
    Their import path may be unchanged, but Go must still find the new nested
    module in the build list. Where the parent serves as a compatibility
    umbrella, have it require the nested module at the shared release version;
    otherwise document the new module requirement for consumers.
    Tell consumers to upgrade the parent requirement to the first split-aware
    release before adding the new nested module themselves. A local consumer
    test that mixed `github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils v1.170.7` with
    `github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/collection` failed with Go's
    `ambiguous import` error because both modules claimed the same package path.
4. Keep `.github/dependabot.yml` coverage, generator `tool` declarations, and
    generated files with the module that now owns each package. Check that
    [CDS](https://github.com/ARMmbed/continuous-delivery-scripts) prepares and
    tags every module in the same project release.

### Preserve an old path when changing imports

If the preferred import path differs from a published one, retain the old
package at its old path. Put the implementation in the preferred package and
make the old package a thin compatibility layer:

```go
package oldapi

import preferred "example.com/project/utils/newapi"

type Decoder = preferred.Decoder

func NewDecoder() *Decoder { return preferred.NewDecoder() }
```

Use type aliases (`type Old = preferred.Type`) for exported types, including
interfaces and option types, so values from either import path have the same
Go type identity. Forward exported functions, including generic helpers, to
the preferred implementation. Constants can refer to the preferred constants.
Remove duplicate implementations and generators from the compatibility package;
keep its import path and document the preferred one. Keep the dependency
direction from old to preferred to avoid import cycles.

Go has no true alias for an exported variable. If consumers can reassign one,
copying its value into a second variable does not preserve shared state. Review
such APIs individually rather than assuming that a wrapper preserves their
behaviour.

### Verify compatibility

- Compile and test both the preferred and old imports, including callers that
  use values from the two packages together. Compile-time assignments can
  confirm that exported types really are aliases.
- Run `go generate`, lint, and tests for each affected module with the project's
  build tags. Check modules independently with `GOWORK=off go test ./...` and
  `GOWORK=off go mod download`.
- Verify that every `go.mod` appears in `go.work`, that internal requirements
  point to the shared release version, and that the release publishes the
  modules consumers need. See the [Go modules guide](https://arm-software.github.io/golang-utils/guides/go-modules.html) for the
  repository's workspace and CI commands.

For an import-path migration in this repository, see the
[serialisation packages guide](https://arm-software.github.io/golang-utils/guides/migrations/serialisation.html).


## Use serialisation packages

<!--
Copyright (C) 2020-2026 Arm Limited or its affiliates and Contributors. All rights reserved.
SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
-->

Use `github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/serialisation`
module for new applications. After the next project-wide
[CDS](https://github.com/ARMmbed/continuous-delivery-scripts) release, add it
to a Go project with:

```bash
go get github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/serialisation@latest
```

For example, import its XML helper as
`github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/serialisation/xml`. The same
spelling applies to the JSON, YAML, maps, slice and frontmatter subpackages:

| New import path suffix | Historical import path suffix |
| --- | --- |
| `/serialisation` | `/serialization` |
| `/serialisation/xml` | `/serialization/xml` |
| `/serialisation/json` | `/serialization/json` |
| `/serialisation/yaml` | `/serialization/yaml` |
| `/serialisation/maps` | `/serialization/maps` |
| `/serialisation/slice` | `/serialization/slice` |
| `/serialisation/frontmatter` | `/serialization/frontmatter` |
| `/serialisation/json/frontmatter` | `/serialization/json/frontmatter` |
| `/serialisation/yaml/frontmatter` | `/serialization/yaml/frontmatter` |
| `/serialisation/maps/testing` | `/serialization/maps/testing` |

The JSON and YAML frontmatter subpackages are separate Go modules. Depend on
the specific module you import, for example
`go get github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils/serialisation/json/frontmatter@latest`.

If a consumer still requires a pre-split umbrella version such as
`github.com/ARM-software/golang-utils/utils v1.170.7`, upgrade that umbrella
requirement to the first split-aware release before adding one of the new
individual modules. Mixing a pre-split umbrella version with a split module
causes Go to report an `ambiguous import` error because both modules provide the
same package path.

The legacy packages remain available so existing imports do not need to change
immediately. Their `doc.go` files mark them as deprecated and point to the new
packages. All legacy helpers delegate to their `serialisation` counterparts;
exported types are aliases of the canonical types, including the frontmatter
format and parser types. Values can be used across the two import paths without
conversion.

When migrating, change the import path to its `serialisation` equivalent.

Both module paths are listed in `go.work` and participate in one [CDS](https://github.com/ARMmbed/continuous-delivery-scripts)
release.



## API reference

- [Generated API reference](https://arm-software.github.io/golang-utils/api.html)
